## Purpose
FastAPI routes for the IDE-to-browser "flowin-handoff" feature: an IDE-side client posts a task + transcript + repo URL to mint a one-time handoff session, the user opens the returned URL in a browser to inspect it, and a separate endpoint kicks off the pipeline as a fire-and-forget background task whose progress streams over a WebSocket.

## Shape
- `receive_handoff` (`POST /api/handoff/receive`) — API-key authenticated; creates a `HandoffSession` row and returns a one-time browser URL.
- `get_handoff` (`GET /api/handoff/{token}`) — JWT-authenticated, issuer-only; lazily flips expired `pending`/`running` sessions to `expired`/`failed`.
- `start_handoff` (`POST /api/handoff/{token}/start`) — JWT-authenticated; decrypts the user's stored GitHub PAT, does an atomic conditional `UPDATE` to claim the run (guards against a double-click/two-tab race), and schedules `_run_pipeline_background` via `asyncio.create_task`.
- `_run_pipeline_background` — drives `run_handoff_pipeline`'s async generator, dispatches each event over the WebSocket (`app.api.websocket_handoff.dispatch_event`, imported locally to avoid a cycle), and persists the final status/PR info with a fresh DB session since the request session is gone by completion time.
- Pydantic schemas (`HandoffReceiveRequest/Response`, `HandoffSessionView`, `HandoffStartResponse`) and small helpers (`_mint_token`, `_now`, `_aware`, `_serialise`, `_user_has_pat`).

## Why this shape
The endpoint returns immediately (202-style fire-and-forget) because the pipeline itself is long-running and its live progress is meant to flow over the WebSocket channel rather than block the HTTP response; the atomic conditional UPDATE in `start_handoff` and the background task's own DB session are both explicit guards against races and request-scope teardown, per their inline comments.
